questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What is recursion? (1 mark)

(b) Give ONE example of a recursive function. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Recursion (1 mark)**

Recursion is a programming technique in which a **function (or procedure) calls itself** to solve a problem by reducing it to a smaller problem of the same kind. A recursive function must have a **base case** (a stopping condition that is solved directly); without it the function would call itself for ever.

**(b) Example of a recursive function (1 mark)**

The **factorial** function, $n! = n \times (n-1)!$ with the base case $0! = 1$ (and $1! = 1$):

```c
int factorial(int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;                 /* base case */
    return n * factorial(n - 1);  /* recursive call */
}
```

For example `factorial(5)` calls `factorial(4)`, ..., `factorial(1)` and returns $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$. (The logic was checked with an equivalent Python function, which gives `factorial(5) = 120`; the C code was not compiled.) Another example is the Fibonacci function.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Almost all organizations have computer-based information system.

(a) Give TWO advantages of an information system to a business organization. (2 marks)

(b) Identify and explain the THREE levels of the organizational hierarchy. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Two advantages of an information system (2 marks)**

- It **processes and retrieves data quickly and accurately**, which reduces errors and the time spent on routine work (invoices, payroll, stock).
- It gives managers **accurate and up-to-date information** (reports and summaries) that **supports decision making**, and it improves the communication between the departments.
- (Other valid answers: a lower operating cost; a competitive advantage; secure storage of the data.)

**(b) The three levels of the organisational hierarchy (3 marks)**

| Level | Who | What is done and what information is used |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategic level** (top management) | Directors and senior managers | They take the **long-term decisions**, set the objectives and the policy of the organisation; they use summarised information and reports on trends and on the external environment. |
| **Tactical level** (middle management) | Heads of departments and managers | They **plan and control the use of resources in the medium term** (budgets, targets) to carry out the strategy; they use summary reports, comparisons of results with plans. |
| **Operational level** (lower management and workers) | Supervisors, clerks, operators | They carry out the **day-to-day routine tasks** (sales, payments, stock, production); they use detailed transaction data. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
A software development schedule is shown in the table below.

| Task | Description | Duration (working days) | Predecessor(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Requirement Analysis; | 5 | -------------- |
| B | Systems Design | 15 | A |
| C | Programming | 25 | B |
| D | Telecoms | 15 | B |
| E | Hardware Installation | 30 | B |
| F | Integration | 10 | C, D |
| G | System Testing | 10 | E, F |
| H | Training/Support | 5 | G |
| I | Handover | 5 | H |

(a) Draw the PERT chart for this project. (4 marks)

(b) Determine the critical path of this project. (2 marks)

(c) Give TWO slack tasks, stating their slack times. (2 marks)

(d) Give TWO characteristics you will use to determine that a project was good. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) PERT chart (4 marks)**

Each task is drawn as an arrow (with its duration) between two numbered events (circles). Task F needs both C and D, so a **dummy activity** (duration 0, dotted arrow) is used to join the end of D to event 4. The earliest time **E** of an event is the largest sum of durations along the paths that reach it (forward pass); the latest time **L** is found by working backwards from the finish time of 75 days (backward pass).

![fig-1](gce-al-ict-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

| Event | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Earliest time E | 0 | 5 | 20 | 45 | 35 | 55 | 65 | 70 | 75 |
| Latest time L | 0 | 5 | 20 | 45 | 45 | 55 | 65 | 70 | 75 |

**(b) Critical path (2 marks)**

The paths from the start to the end are (checked by a script):

- A - B - C - F - G - H - I: $5 + 15 + 25 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 75$ days;
- A - B - E - G - H - I: $5 + 15 + 30 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 70$ days;
- A - B - D - F - G - H - I: $5 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 65$ days.

The longest path is the **critical path: A - B - C - F - G - H - I, 75 working days**, which is the minimum duration of the project. These tasks have zero slack.

**(c) Two slack tasks (2 marks)**

The slack (float) of a task = latest start - earliest start.

| Task | Earliest start | Earliest finish | Latest start | Latest finish | Slack |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 5 | 0 | 5 | 0 |
| B | 5 | 20 | 5 | 20 | 0 |
| C | 20 | 45 | 20 | 45 | 0 |
| D | 20 | 35 | 30 | 45 | **10** |
| E | 20 | 50 | 25 | 55 | **5** |
| F | 45 | 55 | 45 | 55 | 0 |
| G | 55 | 65 | 55 | 65 | 0 |
| H | 65 | 70 | 65 | 70 | 0 |
| I | 70 | 75 | 70 | 75 | 0 |

The two slack tasks are **D (Telecoms) with a slack of 10 days** and **E (Hardware Installation) with a slack of 5 days**.

**(d) Two characteristics of a good project (2 marks)**

- It was **completed on time**, within the planned schedule (75 working days).
- It was completed **within the budget** and the final system **meets the user requirements** with good quality (it works correctly, the users were trained and are satisfied).
